topic: Null safety II: smart casts, is & as

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: After `x is String` succeeds, `x` is smart cast to `String` inside that branch, so `uppercase()` is available without an explicit cast. `42` fails the check and takes the `else` branch.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.code:
val x: Any = "42"
val n = x as Int
println(n + 1)
questions.explanation: `as` is an unsafe cast. It never converts a value, it only checks the runtime type. `x` holds a `String`, so the cast to `Int` throws `ClassCastException`. To parse the text you need `toInt()`, which is the only thing that would throw `NumberFormatException`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `as?` is the safe cast: when the type doesn't match it returns `null` instead of throwing. The elvis operator then replaces that `null` with "none".

questions.question: This code compiles.
questions.explanation: Generic type arguments are erased at runtime, so the JVM can't check `List<String>`. The compiler reports "cannot check for instance of erased type". Use `x is List<*>` instead, or a `reified` type parameter in an inline function.

questions.question: Inside an Activity's `onCreate`, what is the type of `id`?
questions.explanation: `return` is an expression of type `Nothing`, which is a subtype of every type. The common type of `String?`'s non-null part and `Nothing` is `String`, so `id` is non-null for the rest of the function. `Nothing` is only the type of the right-hand side, not of the whole expression.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because the `!is` branch returns, the compiler knows that `x` must be a `String` on the lines after it, so `x.length` compiles. `3` is not a `String`, so it returns -1. Its digit count is never computed.

questions.question: Why doesn't this compile?
options: `s` is a `var` member, so it could change between the check and the use
Smart casts never work on class properties, only on local variables, even for a `val`
`!= null` checks can't produce smart casts. You need `is String`
`Box` must be a data class for its properties to be smart cast
questions.explanation: The compiler can't guarantee that a `var` member property keeps its value between the check and the use. Smart casts do work on stable `val` properties in the same module. Fix it by copying to a local (`val s = b.s`) or by using `b.s?.length`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `||` only evaluates its right side when `s == null` is false, so `s` is smart cast to `String` there. The `else` branch runs only when both conditions are false, which means `s` is non-null there too.

questions.question: After `if (obj.prop != null)`, in which cases is a smart cast of `obj.prop` to non-null IMPOSSIBLE? Select all that apply.
options: `prop` is a `val` with a custom getter
`prop` is a public `val` declared in a different module (e.g. a library)
`prop` is a plain `val` with no custom getter, declared in the same module
`prop` is a `private val` of the same class
questions.explanation: A smart cast needs a stable value. A `var` can change, an `open` or custom getter may return something different on each call, and a library could later change a property from another module. A final `val` with a backing field in the same module is stable, so it can be smart cast.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `x` holds a boxed `Long`, and a `Long` is not an `Int`. Casts never convert numbers, so `as?` returns `null` and the elvis operator produces -1. Use `(x as? Number)?.toInt()` to convert.

questions.question: `context.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE)` returns `Any!` (Java `Object`). Which line gives you a `ConnectivityManager?` without ever throwing?
questions.explanation: Only `as?` yields `null` when the type is wrong or the value is null. `as ConnectivityManager?` allows null but still throws `ClassCastException` on a wrong type, and the other two throw on null. With core-ktx you can write `context.getSystemService<ConnectivityManager>()`.

questions.question: This code compiles, because `name` is a local variable checked right before use.
questions.explanation: Normally a local `var` can be smart cast. Here, though, it is assigned inside a lambda, and the lambda could run at any time, even on another thread. The compiler reports that `name` "is mutated in a capturing closure". A lambda that only reads `name` would not block the smart cast.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `null` is a valid value of the nullable type `String?`, so the cast succeeds and `s` is `null`. Casting `null` with `as String` (non-null target) would throw instead.

questions.question: A Fragment uses this code in `onAttach`. What happens if the host Activity does NOT implement `MyListener`?
options: It throws IllegalStateException with the custom message in `onAttach`
`listener` is set to null, and the app crashes later when a callback is invoked
It doesn't compile, because `throw` can't be used as the right side of `?:`
questions.explanation: `as?` returns null on a type mismatch, never `ClassCastException`. The elvis operator then evaluates `throw`, which has type `Nothing`, so it is a valid right-hand side. The app fails fast in `onAttach` with a clear message, and `listener` can be a non-null type.

questions.question: This compiles: after `requireNotNull(s)` the compiler smart casts `s` to `String`, even though its return value is ignored.
questions.explanation: `requireNotNull` declares a contract saying it returns only if its argument is non-null. That lets the compiler smart cast `s` afterwards. The same applies to `checkNotNull`, `require(s != null)` and `check(s != null)`.

questions.question: Which of these calls throw `IllegalStateException`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The `check` family and `error()` signal an invalid object or program state, so they throw `IllegalStateException`. The `require` family validates arguments passed by the caller and throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

questions.question: A Java method `public String getName()` has no nullability annotations and returns null at runtime. What happens in Kotlin?
questions.code:
val user = JavaUser()
val a = user.getName()      // line 1
val b: String = user.getName() // line 2
options: Line 1 types `a` as `String!`, and line 2 throws NPE right away
Both lines fail to compile until you add `?` or `!!`
Both lines succeed, and the crash happens only when `b.length` is called
Line 1 is inferred as `String?`, and line 2 is a compile error
questions.explanation: Unannotated Java types become platform types (`String!`). Kotlin lets you treat them as either nullable or non-null and does not check nullability at compile time. When you assign one to a declared non-null type, Kotlin inserts a runtime null check, so line 2 throws NPE right there. `a` stays `String!`, which can blow up much later. That delay is why it's safer to declare such values as `String?` explicitly.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because of type erasure, the runtime can only check `x is List`, so the cast succeeds with just an "unchecked cast" warning. Calling `size` never touches the elements. The `ClassCastException` would happen only when an element is used as a `String`, for example `val s: String = strs[0]`.

questions.question: What happens when this is compiled with Kotlin 2.x (the K2 compiler) and run?
options: Compile error: unresolved reference `length`, because the check isn't inside the `if`
It compiles only if `isStr` is declared `const`
questions.explanation: K2 keeps track of what a local `val` holding a type check implies, so `if (isStr)` smart casts `x` to `String`. The old K1 compiler rejected this code, which is why many older answers online say it fails.

questions.question: What does this print with kotlinc 2.x (K2)?
questions.explanation: After `x is Cat || x is Dog`, K2 smart casts `x` to the closest common supertype, `Named`, so `x.name` resolves and prints "Tom". K1 couldn't do this and reported an unresolved reference.
